In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth is all a blessing from Allah, and He is the one truly deserving that He be praised and extolled on account of it. When He said, "Praise belongs to Allah" (al-Fatiha 1), and then described His essence as the bestower of all worldly blessings, its meaning became: He is the one to be praised for the blessings of this world, just as you say, "Praise your brother who clothed you and carried you," meaning: praise him for his clothing you and carrying you.

When He said, "And to Him belongs praise in the Hereafter" (al-Saba' 1), it became known that He is the one to be praised for the blessings of the Hereafter, which is the reward. If you ask: what is the difference between the two praises? I say: As for praise in this world, it is obligatory, because it is for a blessing bestowed as a favour, and it is the path to attaining the blessing of the Hereafter, which is the reward. As for praise in the Hereafter, it is not obligatory [[Mahmud said: "The first praise is obligatory because it is for a blessing bestowed as a favour; the second is not obligatory, because it is for a blessing that is obligatory upon the Benefactor." Ahmad said: The truth regarding the difference between the two praises is that the first is a worship for which one is accountable, while the second is not something one is accountable for nor required to do; rather, in the second creation it is like the instinctive matters in the first creation. For this reason the Prophet (peace be upon him) said, "They are inspired to glorify (Allah) just as they are inspired to breathe." Otherwise, the first blessing is like the second, by the grace of Allah Most High upon His servants, not by way of entitlement. And Allah is the Granter of success.]], because it is for a blessing that must be delivered to its rightful recipient [[The phrase "a blessing that must be delivered to its rightful recipient" is based on the doctrine of the Mu'tazila. As for the People of the Sunna, they do not hold that anything is obligatory upon Allah, and praise is not obligatory in the Hereafter, because it is not an abode of obligation. (Ibn Ghalib?)]]. It is rather a completion of the joy of the believers and a fulfilment of their delight:

They take pleasure in it as the thirsty take pleasure in cold water [[The phrase "as the thirsty take pleasure" — in al-Sihah, "al-atash" is a condition that afflicts a person: he drinks water but is not satisfied. (Ibn Ghalib?)]].

"And He is the All-Wise," who perfected the affairs of both abodes and arranged them by His wisdom, "the All-Aware," of every existing thing that will come to be.

Then He mentioned, from among what He encompasses in knowledge, "what enters into the earth," such as the rain, as in His saying, "then He made it flow as springs in the earth" (al-Zumar 21), and such as treasures, hidden stores, and the dead, and all that the earth gathers. "And what comes out of it," such as trees and plants, the water of springs, crops, animals, and other things. "And what descends from the heaven," such as rains, snow, hail, thunderbolts, provisions, angels, and various kinds of blessings and decrees, as He, the Exalted, said, "And in the heaven is your provision and what you are promised" (al-Dhariyat 22). "And what ascends into it," such as angels and the deeds of servants. "And He is the Most Merciful, the Forgiving," despite the abundance of His blessings and the completeness of His bounty, toward those who fall short in discharging the obligations of thanking Him.

And Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) recited: "nunazzilu" (with the nun and with the doubled zay).

Their saying, "The Hour will not come upon us," is a denial of resurrection and a rejection of the Hour's arrival. Or it expresses impatience at what they had been promised regarding its establishment, in a mocking and derisive manner, like their saying, "When is this promise?"

The affirmation that follows the negation is introduced with "Bala" (Yes indeed), meaning: the matter is nothing but the Hour's coming. Then this affirmation is repeated, emphasized by what is the utmost in emphasis and intensity, namely swearing by God, Mighty and Majestic. Then the oath is further strengthened by what follows the one sworn by, namely the attributes ascribed to Him, up to His words, "that He may recompense" (li-yajziya). This is because the greatness of the state of the one sworn by indicates the strength of the state of what is sworn to, and its firmness and steadfastness, since it stands in the position of calling upon a witness for the matter. Whenever the one called as witness is higher in standing, more excellent in merit, and loftier in rank, the testimony is stronger and more emphatic, and what is attested is more established and firmly rooted.

If you say: Is there a particular connection between the attribute by which the one sworn by is described and this meaning? I say: Yes. The establishment of the Hour is among the most prominent of the unseen matters and the most hidden of them, and the first to come to mind when one hears "Knower of the Unseen." So when He swore by His name to establish the Hour's establishment, and that it will certainly occur, and then described Himself by what pertains to knowledge of the unseen, that nothing of the hidden is beyond His knowledge, and including within this His comprehensive knowledge of the time of the Hour's establishment, the connection you seek came out clearly.

If you say: The people denied and rejected the Hour's coming. Suppose He swore to them with the most severe oaths and insisted on the oath with utmost effort; how can the oath of one whom they consider a liar against God be valid for what they denied? I say: This would be so if He had confined Himself to the oath and not followed it with the decisive proof and the clear evidence, which is His words "that He may recompense." God has placed in the intellects and instilled in the natural dispositions the necessity of recompense [[His words "and instilled in the natural dispositions the necessity of recompense": this is what wisdom requires, though according to the People of the Sunnah nothing is obligatory upon God Most High; so reflect. (Editor)]], and that the good-doer must have a reward and the wrongdoer must have a punishment. His words "that He may recompense" are connected to His words "it will surely come upon you" as a reason for it. It is read "latatiyannakum" with the letter ta and with ya. The reading with ya: its pronoun may refer to the Hour in the sense of the Day, or it may be ascribed to the Knower of the Unseen, meaning that His command will come upon you, as He said, "Do they await anything but that the angels should come to them, or that your Lord should come?" and He said, "Or that the command of your Lord should come."

It is also read "ʿĀlim al-ghayb" and "ʿAllām al-ghayb," in the genitive as an attribute of "my Lord." And "ʿĀlim al-ghayb" and "ʿĀlim al-ghuyub" in the nominative, as a laudatory epithet.

"Wa-la yaʿzub" is read with a dammah and a kasrah on the zay, from al-ʿuzūb, which means distance. It is said: a "ʿazīb" meadow, far from people. "Mithqāla dharratin": the measure of the smallest ant. "Dhālika": a reference to the weight of an atom. It is also read "wa-lā aṣghara min dhālika wa-lā akbara," in the nominative on the basis of the inchoative, and in the accusative as a negation of the genus, like your saying "lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-llāh," in the nominative and accusative. This is a sentence disconnected from what precedes it. If you say: Can the nominative be coordinated with "mithqāla dharratin," as if it were said: "Nothing escapes Him of the weight of an atom, nor anything smaller or greater, and an addition, not for emphasizing the negation"? And can the accusative be coordinated with "dharratin," being in the accusative place of the genitive because it is not declined, as if it were said: "Nothing escapes Him of the weight of an atom, nor of a weight smaller than that, nor greater"? I say: The particle of exception forbids that, unless you make the pronoun in "ʿanhu" refer to the Unseen and make "al-ghayb" the name of the hidden things, before they are written in the Preserved Tablet, because their being recorded in the Tablet is a kind of emergence from concealment, in the sense that nothing separates from the Unseen and nothing departs from it except that it is inscribed in the Tablet.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 34, verses 7–8:

﴿Those who disbelieve﴾ are the Quraysh. Some of them said to others: ﴿Shall we point you to a man﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿who will tell you that when you are completely torn apart you will be resurrected in a new creation?﴾ This is one of the wonders of wonders: that you will be raised and brought forth as a new creation after you have become dust and crumbled bones, and that decay will tear your bodies ﴿completely apart﴾, that is, it will scatter you and disperse your parts ﴿with utter dispersal﴾. ﴿Has he invented a lie against Allah, or is there madness in him?﴾ That is, is he fabricating falsehood about Allah in what he attributes to Him concerning this, or is there madness in him that makes him imagine it and puts it on his tongue? Then Allah, glorified is He, said: Muhammad is in no way guilty of fabrication or madness; he is free of both. Rather, it is these disbelievers who deny the resurrection who are ﴿in the torment of the Fire﴾ and in what leads them to it of misguidance from the truth, while they are heedless of it. That is the greatest and most overpowering madness upon their minds. He made their being in torment a consequence of their being in error, as if the two existed at the same time, because misguidance, whose necessary result and requirement is torment, is in reality joined with it.

Zayd ibn Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) read: ﴿yunabbi'kum﴾ (he informs you).

If you say: you have made ﴿mumazzaq﴾ a verbal noun (maṣdar), as in the line of the Kitab:

"Have you not known the sending forth (musarraḥī) of the rhymes, that I am neither unable (fa-la ʿayyan) with them nor (do I) seize (ijtilāban)?" [This is a line of Jarir, and it is among the verses of the Kitab. The word musarrah is a maṣdar on the pattern of the passive participle, so it means the sending forth (al-tasrīh), that is, the release or the arrangement. "Sarraḥat al-jāriyah shaʿraha" means she combed it, so it flowed loose and became beautiful. It is annexed to the agent-noun (bāʾ al-fāʿil) ... The word al-qawafi is the object, and the ʿayy is put in the accusative because it resembles a noun in annexation, or its tanwin is dropped out of necessity, meaning: I am not unable with them, nor incapable of them, nor do I seize them, nor do I steal them. It is also permissible that ʿayy here means weakness of meaning. Al-ijtilab means concealment, from jalbat al-jurh, which is the covering skin that conceals it. "Fihinna" means "fi hinna" (in them).]

Could it then be a place? I say: yes. Its meaning is what has come to be of the dead in the bellies of birds and beasts, what the floods have carried away in every direction, and what the winds have scattered and cast in every place. If you ask: what governs ﴿idha﴾ (when)? I answer: what is indicated by ﴿innakum lafi khalqin jadid﴾ (indeed you are in a new creation), and its like has already been mentioned. If you ask: is ﴿jadid﴾ a form of the active participle or the passive? I answer: according to the Basrans it is in the sense of the active participle, as you say "jadda fahuwa jadid" (it became new, so it is new), like "hadda fahuwa hadid" and "qalla fahuwa qalil". According to the Kufans it is in the sense of the passive participle, from "jaddahu" when he cut it; and they said: it is that which the weaver has just woven in the garment, and then it became common usage. They say: for this reason the Arabs said "milhafa jadid" (a new cloak). According to the Basrans, it is like the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near﴾ and the like. If you ask: why was the hamza dropped in His saying ﴿aftara﴾ but not in His saying ﴿al-sihr﴾, when both are hamzat al-wasl? I answer: the analogy requires dropping it, but a matter compelled them to keep it from being dropped in forms like ﴿ā-sihr﴾, namely the fear that the interrogative would be confused with the declarative, since the hamzat al-wasl is pronounced with fatha, like the interrogative hamza. If you ask: what is the meaning of describing misguidance as ﴿distant﴾ (ba'id)? I answer: it is a metaphorical attribution, because the distant is an attribute of the one who has gone astray when he moves away from the straight road, and the more he moves away from it, the more astray he is.

If you say: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was well known among the Quraysh as a scholar, and his announcement of the resurrection was widespread among them, so what is the meaning of His saying ﴿Shall we point you to a man who will inform you﴾, where they made him indefinite for them and offered to show them how to find him, as one points to an unknown person in an unknown matter? I answer: they intended by this mockery and derision, and they presented it in the manner of playing with some of the riddles that are posed for laughter and amusement, feigning ignorance of him and of his affair.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 34, verse 9:

Have they not looked at the sky and the earth? Wherever they are, and wherever they walk, both are encompassing them before them and behind them. They cannot pass beyond their boundaries or come out of what they are in of the dominion (malakut) of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Have they not feared that Allah might cause the earth to swallow them up or drop upon them fragments of the sky? That is because of their denial of the signs and their disbelief in the Messenger (ﷺ) and in what he brought, just as He did to Qarun and the people of the thicket (al-Aykah).

﴿Indeed, in that is a sign and a lesson for every servant who turns back in repentance﴾. Looking at the sky and the earth, reflecting upon them, and what they indicate of the power of Allah, is a sign and an indication for every servant who turns back (munib), that is, who returns to his Lord and obeys Him, because the one who turns in repentance cannot be free of considering the signs of Allah, and [they indicate] that He is capable of everything, including the resurrection and the punishment of whoever disbelieves in Him.

It is read yashya', and yakhsif and yuskit, with the ya' (third person), in accordance with the saying of the Exalted, ﴿Has he invented a lie against Allah?﴾ (34:8), and with the nun (first person plural) in accordance with His saying, ﴿And We have certainly given﴾ (34:10). The awb means: return with him in glorification, or: return with him in the tasbīh whenever he returns in it, for when he returns it, he has returned in it. The meaning of the glorification of the mountains is that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, creates glorification in them, just as He created speech in the tree, so that they hear from them what one hears from one who glorifies. It was a miracle for Dawud. It was said: he used to lament over his sin with melodious and mournful chanting, and the mountains would aid him in his lament with their echoes [[His words "with their echoes": plural of ṣadā, which is that which answers you with a likeness of your voice in mountains and elsewhere, as in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (Ghulām)]] and the birds with their voices. It is also read "wa-l-ṭayr," in the nominative and accusative, as a conjunction with the wording of "mountains" and its position. They also permitted that it be in the accusative as an object with "with him," and that it be conjoined to "bounty," in the sense of "and We subjected the birds to him." If you ask: what is the difference between this arrangement and saying, "We indeed gave Dawud a bounty from Us: the mountains and the birds re-echoing praise with him"?

I say: there is a great difference between them. Do you not see the grandeur in it that cannot be hidden, in indicating the might of lordship and the majesty of divinity, where the mountains are placed in the position of rational beings who, when He commands them, obey and submit, and when He calls them, hear and respond. This is an indication that there is no animal, inanimate thing, speaker or silent thing, except that it is subject to His will and not beyond His command. "And We made iron soft for him": We made it pliable like clay, dough and wax, which he shapes with his hand however he wishes, without fire or striking with a hammer. It was said: the iron became soft in his hand because of the strength of power he had been given. It is read ṣābighāt, which are the wide, flowing coats of mail, and he was the first to make them; before that they were plates. It was said: he used to sell a coat of mail for four thousand, and spend from it on himself and his dependents, and give charity to the poor. It was said: when he became king of the Children of Israel, he used to go out disguised, asking people about himself, saying to them, "What do you say about Dawud?" They would praise him. So Allah sent him an angel in the form of a human, and he asked him as was his habit. He said, "A good man, were it not for one trait in him." "Dawud's fear." He asked, "What is it?" He said, "Were it not that he feeds his dependents from the public treasury." At that, he asked his Lord to provide for him a means by which he could be independent of the public treasury, so He taught him the craft of making coats of mail. "And measure in the links": do not make the rivets fine, lest they be loose, nor coarse, lest they break the rings. "Al-sard" is the weaving of coats of mail. "And work righteousness": the pronoun refers to Dawud and his family. "And We subjected the wind to Sulayman": according to the one who reads it in the accusative, "and the wind to Sulayman, subjected"; according to the one who reads it in the nominative, and likewise according to the one who reads "al-riyāḥ" in the nominative. "Its morning course is a month's journey": its course in the morning is a month's journey, and its course in the evening is likewise. It is read: "ghudwatuhā wa-rawḥatuhā." It is related from al-Ḥasan, may Allah be pleased with him, that he would set out in the morning and take his midday rest at Iṣṭakhr, then set out in the afternoon and his evening be in Kābul. It is related that one of them saw written in a dwelling in the region of the Tigris, written by one of Sulayman's companions: "We alighted here and did not build it, and we found it built. We set out from Iṣṭakhr in the morning and said it, and we are departing from it and will pass the night in Syria, if Allah wills." "Al-qiṭr" is molten copper from qiṭrān. If you ask: what did he mean by the spring of molten copper? I say: he meant the copper ore, but He caused it to flow for him [[His words "but He caused it to flow" perhaps: caused it to flow for him (Ghulām)]] just as He softened iron for Dawud, so it gushed forth as water gushes from a spring, and therefore He named it "spring of molten copper" by the name of what it became, as He said: "Indeed I see myself pressing wine." It was said: it flowed for three days each month. "By the permission of his Lord": by His command. "And whoever of them deviates": whoever turns aside from "Our command," which We commanded him, from obedience to Sulayman. It is read "yazigh," from azāghahu. "The punishment of the blaze": the punishment of the Hereafter, according to Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both. And according to al-Suddī: there was with him an angel with a whip of fire; whenever one of them disobeyed him, he struck him from where the jinn could not see.

"Al-maḥārīb": dwellings and noble assemblies protected from being degraded; they were called maḥārīb because they are defended and guarded. It was said: they are mosques. "Al-tamāthīl": images of angels, prophets and righteous people, which were made in mosques of copper, brass, glass and marble, so that people would see them and worship in the manner of their worship. If you ask: how did Sulayman, peace be upon him, permit the making of images? I say: this is among matters in which the revealed laws may differ, since it is not among the things the intellect finds repugnant, like injustice and lying. It is related from Abū al-ʿĀliya: making images was not then forbidden. It is also possible that they were not images of living beings, such as images of trees and other things, since a "timthāl" is anything fashioned in the likeness of something else, living or not. Or images with their heads removed. It is related that they made for him two lions at the base of his throne and two eagles above it; when he wished to ascend, the two lions would extend their forelegs for him, and when he sat, the two eagles would shade him with their wings. "Al-jawābī": large basins. He said:

*"They go out to the family of al-Muḥalliq with a bowl like the Iraqi canal's flow, overflowing."* [[Al-Aʿshā's praise of al-Muḥalliq. It is also related as "tulūḥ" instead of "tarūḥ," because it appears when it comes out of the house at the start of the day, rising above them. "Al-jafna": the dish of crumbled bread. "Al-jābiya": the basin into which water is collected, that is, gathered into the basin. "Al-saiḥ": abundant flowing water. "Fahaqa yafhaqu," like faraḥa yafraḥu: it expanded, filled and overflowed. From it the hadith: that he stood at the gate of Paradise and it was opened wide for him, that is, it opened and expanded. "Al-mutafayhiq" is one who speaks much. So his words "tafhaq" mean it fills while expanding until it nearly overflows.]]

because the water is gathered in it, that is, collected. The verb is attributed to it figuratively, and it is one of the dominant attributes like "dābba." It was said: a thousand men would sit on one basin. It is read with the omission of the yā', relying on the kasra, like His saying: "the day the caller calls."

"Rāsiyāt": fixed, established on their cooking-pots, not moving from them because of their largeness. "Work, family of Dawud": a narration of what was said to the family of Dawud. "Shukran" is in the accusative as an object of purpose: that is, work for Allah and worship Him in the manner of gratitude for His favours. In it is evidence that worship must be performed in the way of thankfulness. Or it is in the accusative of circumstance: thankful. Or with an implied verb: "give thanks, thanks," since "work" contains the meaning of "give thanks," in that working for the benefactor is thanks to him. It may also be in the accusative as a direct object of "work"; its meaning: We subjected the jinn to you, they work for you whatever you wish, so you work, giving thanks, in the manner of correspondence. "Al-shakūr": one who devotes himself to giving thanks, expending his utmost effort in it, whose heart, tongue and limbs are occupied with it, in belief, acknowledgment and striving, and most of his time. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both: one who gives thanks for all his states. It is related from al-Suddī: one who gives thanks for being thankful. It was said: one who sees his inability to give thanks. It is related from Dawud that he divided the hours of the night and day among his family, so that no hour would pass but that a person from the family of Dawud was standing in prayer. It is related from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he heard a man say, "O Allah, make me of the few," and ʿUmar said, "What is this supplication?" The man said, "I heard Allah say: 'And few of My servants are the thankful,' so I ask Him to make me of those few." ʿUmar said, "Everyone is more knowledgeable than ʿUmar." [[Narrated by Ibn Abī Shayba and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Aḥmad in the Zawāʾid al-Zuhd, from the narration of al-Taymī, who said: ʿUmar said — and mentioned something similar.]]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 34, verse 14:

It is recited: ﴿Then when We decreed death upon him﴾. "Dabbat al-ard" (the creature of the earth) is the termite (al-ardah), the small insect called al-sarfah. "Al-ard" is its action, so it was attributed to it. One says: أرضت الخشبة أرضا (aradat al-khashaba ardan) when the termites have eaten the wood. It is also recited with a fatha on the ra', from أرضت الخشبة أرضا, which is of the pattern فعلته ففعل (fa'altuhu fa'ala), like your saying: أكلت القوادح الأسنان أكلا (akalat al-qawadih al-asnana aklan), "the decay ate the teeth, eating." "Al-minsa'ah" is the staff, because one drives (yansa') and delays with it, meaning he drives away and postpones. It is also recited with a fatha on the mim and with the hamza lightened, by substitution (qalb) and by deletion (hadhf). Both are not analogical, but the analogical lightening is to pronounce the hamza between its two positions (ikhraj al-hamza bayn bayn). "Minsa'atuhu" is on the pattern مفعالة (mif'alah), as one says in al-mida'ah, mida'ah. "Min sa'atihi," meaning from the end of his staff, is called sa'ah, "the bow's sa'ah" (sy'at al-qaws) by metaphor. There are two dialects for it, like their saying: قحة وقحة (qahhah wa-qahhah). [[Note: "like their saying qahhah and qahhah" means kasi'ah and kamidah, in the sense of al-waqahah, which is hardness.]] It is also recited: أكلت منسأته (akalat minsa'atahu), "the termite ate his staff."

﴿The jinn saw clearly﴾. "Tabayyana" means that a thing became manifest and clear. "An" with its clause is a substitute for "al-jinn", the substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal, substitution in which the second term is included in the first), like your saying: تبين زيد جهله (tabayyana Zayd jahluhu), "Zayd's ignorance became clear." Its meaning is that the manifestation is for them: it became clear that ﴿if the jinn had known the unseen, they would not have remained in the humiliating punishment﴾, or: the jinn all came to know clearly, after the matter had been confused for their common people and weak ones and their imaginings, that their great ones were truthful in their claim to know the unseen. Or: those among them who claimed knowledge of the unseen came to know their own incapacity, and that they do not know the unseen, although they had been aware of their own condition before that. It is intended only as mockery of them, as you mock one who claims falsehood when his argument is refuted (دحضت حجته, dahadat hujjatuhu), and his nullity has become evident, by your saying: هل تبينت أنك مبطل؟ (hal tabayyanta annaka mubtil?), "Have you clearly seen that you are a liar?"

You know that he always remained so, manifest. It is also recited: تبينت الجن (tabayyanat al-jinn), on the passive form, on the basis that what is made clear in meaning is "an" with what follows it, since it is a substitute. In the recitation of Ubayy: تبينت الإنس (tabayyanat al-ins), "the humans became clear." From al-Dahhak: تباينت الإنس (tabayyanat al-ins), meaning they got to know one another and became mutually aware. The pronoun in ﴿they﴾ refers to the jinn in His saying: ﴿And among the jinn are those who worked before him﴾. That is, the humans knew that if the jinn had been truthful in what they made others imagine of their knowledge of the unseen, they would not have remained. In the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him): تبينت الإنس أن الجن لو كانوا يعلمون الغيب (tabayyanat al-ins anna al-jinna law kanu ya'lamuna al-ghayb), "the humans came to know clearly that if the jinn knew the unseen."

It is related that it was the custom of Sulayman (peace be upon him) to seclude himself for long periods in the mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis. When his term drew near, he would not rise in the morning without seeing in his prayer niche (mihrab) a tree growing, which Allah had made to speak. He would ask it: "For what are you?" And it would tell him for such and such a purpose, until one day he rose and saw the carob tree. He asked it, and it said: "I grew for the ruin of this mosque." He said: "Allah would not ruin it while I am alive. You are the one on whose account will be my death and the ruin of Bayt al-Maqdis." So he uprooted it and planted it in a wall of his and said: "O Allah, hide my death from the jinn, so that people will know that they do not know the unseen." For they used to eavesdrop and deceive humans into thinking they knew the hidden. He said to the Angel of Death: "When you are commanded concerning me, inform me." He said: "I am commanded concerning you, and only an hour of your life remains." He called the devils, and they built for him a palace of glass with no door. He stood praying, leaning on his staff, and his soul was seized while he was leaning on it. The devils used to gather around his prayer niche wherever he prayed, and no devil would look at him in his prayer without being burned. A devil passed by him and did not hear his voice; then he returned and did not hear it; he looked and saw that Sulayman had fallen dead. They opened it for him, and the staff had been eaten by the termite. They wanted to know the time of his death, so they placed the termite on the staff, and it ate from it a measure in a day and a night. They calculated by that measure and found that he had died a year earlier, and they had been working before him while thinking he was alive. Then the people became certain that if they had known the unseen, they would not have remained in punishment for a year.

It is also related that Dawud (peace be upon him) founded the building of Bayt al-Maqdis at the place of Musa's (peace be upon him) tent, and died before completing it. He bequeathed it to Sulayman, who ordered the devils to complete it. When one year of his life remained, he asked that his death be concealed from them until they finished it, and to refute their claim to knowledge of the unseen. It is related that Afridun came to climb his throne, but when he drew near, the two lions struck his leg and broke it, and after that no one dared approach him. Sulayman's lifespan was fifty-three years: he became king at thirteen years old, remained in his kingdom forty years, and began building Bayt al-Maqdis four years into his reign.

﴿لِسَبَإٍ﴾ «Li-Saba'» is read both with the word diptoted (ṣarf) and without it (man'), and the hamza is replaced by an alif. ﴿مَكانِهِمْ﴾ «Maskanihim» (their dwelling) is read with the kaf both fatha and kasra. It means the place where they lived, namely their town and land in which they resided, or the dwelling of each one of them.

It is also read as ﴿مَساكِنِهِمْ﴾ «Masakinihim» (their dwellings). ﴿جَنَّتانِ﴾ «Jannatān» (two gardens) is either in apposition to ﴿آيَةٌ﴾ «āyah» (a sign), or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, with the sense: the sign is two gardens.

The nominative reading implies praise (madḥ), and this is indicated by the reading of the one who reads ﴿جَنَّتَيْنِ﴾ «Jannatayn» in the accusative as an expression of praise. If you ask: what is the meaning of their being a sign? I say: he did not make the two gardens themselves a sign. Rather, he made their story a sign, and that the people of the two gardens turned away from thanking God for them, so He ruined them and replaced them with ﴿خَمْطٍ﴾ «khamṭ» (bitter tamarisk) and ﴿أَثْلٍ﴾ «athl» (a kind of tamarisk): a sign and a lesson for them, so that they would take heed and be admonished and not return to what they had been upon of disbelief and rejection of blessings. It is also permissible to make the two gardens a sign, i.e., an indicator pointing to God, to His power, His generosity, and the obligation to thank Him.

If you ask: how did God glorify the two gardens of the people of Sheba and make them a sign, when there is many a town of the towns of Iraq surrounded by gardens as you wish? I say: He did not intend just two gardens, but rather two groups of gardens: one group on the right of their town and another on its left, each group close to the other and joined together, so that they were like one garden, just as the fertile rural lands and their orchards are. Or He intended the two gardens of each man among them, on the right and left of his dwelling, as the poet said: [the verse is not given in the text].

﴿كُلُوا مِنْ رِزْقِ رَبِّكُمْ﴾ «Eat of the provision of your Lord». This may be a report of what the prophets of God sent to them said to them, or of what the state of affairs said to them (lisān al-ḥāl), or they are deserving of being told this. When He said ﴿كُلُوا مِنْ رِزْقِ رَبِّكُمْ وَاشْكُرُوا لَهُ﴾ «Eat of the provision of your Lord and be grateful to Him», He followed it with ﴿بَلْدَةٌ طَيِّبَةٌ وَرَبٌّ غَفُورٌ﴾ «a good land and a Lord who is Forgiving». That is: this town in which is your provision is a good town, and your Lord who provided for you and sought your thanks is a Forgiving Lord to the one who thanks Him.

From Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: it was the most fertile and best of lands. A woman would go out with a basket (mikattal) on her head, work with her hands and walk among those trees, and the basket would fill with the fruit that fell into it. ﴿طَيِّبَةٌ﴾ «ṭayyibah» (good): it was not salty. It is said: there were no gnats, flies, fleas, scorpions or snakes in it.

It is also read ﴿بَلْدَةٌ طَيِّبَةٌ وَرَبًّا غَفُورًا﴾ «baldatun ṭayyibatun wa-rabban ghafūran» with the accusative as an expression of praise.

From Tha'lab: the meaning is: dwell and worship. ﴿الْعَرِمِ﴾ «al-ʿarim» (the dam). Al-Jurdh (the jerboa-like rodent): the one which bored through the dam against them. The queen Bilqis struck for them by blocking the gap between the two mountains with rock and pitch, thereby holding back the water of the springs and the rains, and she left in it openings to the measure of what they needed for their irrigation. When they became insolent, it was said: God sent to them thirteen prophets who called them to God and reminded them of His blessing upon them, but they denied them and said: we do not know of any blessing of God. God sent the mole (al-khuld) against their dam, and it bored through it from its base, and so He drowned them.

It is also said: ﴿الْعَرِمُ﴾ is the plural of ʿarimah, which is piled stones, and ʿarimah is said of a heap of food. The intended meaning is the embankment (musannāh) which they built as a dam. It is also said: al-ʿarim is the name of the valley. It is also said: al-ʿarim is heavy rain. It is also read ﴿الْعَرْمِ﴾ «al-ʿarm» with the rā' sukūn.

From al-Ḍaḥḥāk: they were in the interval (fatrah) between Jesus and Muhammad (ﷺ).

It is also read ﴿أُكُلٍ﴾ «ukul» with a ḍammah and sukūn, and with tanwīn and with iḍāfah. The ﴿أُكُلٍ﴾ (food/yield) means the fruit. ﴿خَمْطٍ﴾ «khamṭ» means the arak tree (miswak tree). From Abu 'Ubaydah: every thorny tree. Al-Zajjāj said: every plant that takes on a bitter taste so that it cannot be eaten.

﴿أَثْلٍ﴾ «athl» is a tree resembling the tamarisk, larger than it and with better wood.

The reasoning for the one who reads with tanwīn: the original is "dhawātay ukulin ukulin khamṭ" (two gardens of bitter fruit), so the first noun was omitted and the second noun placed in its position. Or the fruit is described as ﴿خَمْطٍ﴾ «bitter», as though it were said: "two gardens of bitter yield." As for the one who reads with iḍāfah, and he is Abu 'Amr alone, it is because the bitter yield has the meaning of the ﴿بَرِيرٍ﴾ «barīr» (the berries of the arak tree), as though it were said: "two gardens of barīr."

﴿أَثْلٍ﴾ and ﴿سِدْرٍ﴾ «sidr» (lote-tree) are coordinated with ﴿أُكُلٍ﴾, not with ﴿خَمْطٍ﴾, because the athl has no food-yield.

It is also read ﴿وَأَثْلًا﴾ «wa-athlan», and ﴿وَشَيْءٍ﴾ «wa-shay'in» with the accusative, coordinated with ﴿جَنَّتَيْنِ﴾. Calling the substitute "two gardens" is for the sake of correspondence (mushākalah), and in it there is a kind of mockery (tahakkum). From al-Ḥasan, may God have mercy on him: he said: ﴿سِدْرٍ﴾ «sidr», because it is the most honourable of what they were given in exchange.

It is also read ﴿وَهَلْ يُجَازَى﴾ «wa-hal yujāzā» (and is there requited?), ﴿وَهَلْ نُجَازِي﴾ «wa-hal nujāzī» with the nūn, and ﴿وَهَلْ يُجَازَى﴾ with the subject being God alone, and ﴿وَهَلْ يُجْزَى﴾ «wa-hal yujzā». The meaning: such a requital is only deserved by the disbeliever, which is swift punishment. It is said: the believer's evil deeds are expiated by his good deeds, while the disbeliever's deeds are nullified, so he is requited for all the evil he did.

There is another aspect: requital (al-jazā') is general to every recompense. It is used sometimes in the sense of punishment and sometimes in the sense of reward. Since it was used in the sense of punishment in His saying ﴿جَزَيْنَاهُمْ بِمَا كَفَرُوا﴾ «We requited them for their disbelief», meaning: We punished them for their disbelief, it was said: ﴿وَهَلْ نُجَازِي إِلَّا الْكَفُورَ﴾ «and do We requite any but the ungrateful» in the sense of: is anyone punished except...? This is the correct aspect.

It is not valid for anyone to say: why was it said "and is requited none but the ungrateful," given that the requital is restricted to the ungrateful while requital is general to the disbeliever and the believer? For He did not intend general requital, but intended the specific, which is punishment. Indeed it is not permissible that generality be intended here, since it is not its place. Do you not see that if you said: "We requited them for what they disbelieved, and none is requited but the disbeliever and the believer," it would be incorrect and would not complete the sentence? Thus it becomes clear that the objection that might be imagined is baseless, and that the correct view, which admits of no other, is what the speech of God has come upon, "which falsehood cannot approach from before it or from behind it."

The towns which We had blessed: these are the towns of al-Sham (Greater Syria). ﴿Towns which were visible﴾, close to one another, so that one could see another because of their proximity, and so they were visible to those who looked. Or, ﴿lying along the road﴾: visible to the travellers (al-sabila), not so far from their routes that they would be hidden from them.

﴿And We determined therein the travel﴾. It was said: the one who set out in the morning would take his midday rest in one town, and the one who set out in the afternoon would spend the night in another town, until he reached al-Sham, fearing neither hunger, nor thirst, nor an enemy, and needing to carry no provisions or water.

﴿Travel therein﴾, and We said to them, "Travel": there is no saying here, but when they were enabled to travel and its means were made easy for them, it was as though they had been commanded to do so and had been given permission for it.

If you say: what is the meaning of His words ﴿nights and days﴾? I say: its meaning is, travel therein, whether you wish by night or whether you wish by day, for safety therein does not vary with the variation of times. Or: travel therein secure, not fearing, even if the duration of your journey is prolonged and extends for days and nights. Or: travel therein your nights and your days for the duration of your lives, for you are in every time and every era, meeting nothing therein but safety.

It was read: ﴿Our Lord, make the distances between our journeys far﴾, and "bā'id" (far) in the imperative as a call, "O our Lord," for supplication. They were ungrateful for the blessing, became weary (bathirū) of the good life, and grew tired of well-being, so they sought hardship and toil, just as the Children of Israel sought onions and garlic in place of the manna and quails. They said: if the fruit of our gardens were farther away, it would be more fitting that we should desire it. They wished that God would place between them and al-Sham deserts, so that they might ride their mounts through them and take provisions. So God granted them their answer.

It was also read: ﴿Our Lord, bā'ad (made far) between our journeys﴾, and "ba'ada" (made far) between our journeys, as a call, with the verb attributed to "bayn" (between) and its being raised by it, as you say: "sayr farsakhān" (a journey of two farsakhs), and "bū'ida bayna asfārinā". It was also read: ﴿Our Lord, make far﴾ and ﴿between our journey﴾. And "ba'ada" with the ﴿Our Lord﴾ raised as the subject (mubtada'), and the meaning is different from the first, namely, that they found their journeys too short and too near, because of the excess of their luxury and ease, as though they were lamenting (yatashājūn) to their Lord and grieving (yataḥazzanūn) over Him.

﴿Tales﴾: people speak of them and marvel at their conditions, and ﴿We dispersed them completely﴾, a dispersal which people made a proverbial example. They say: "they went the hands of Saba'," and "they scattered in the manner of Saba'." Kuthayyir said:

"Ayādī Saba', O Izza, I was not after you
so the eyes were not pleased by any sight after you."

(Kuthayyir, the companion of Izza. Saba' was a town of great fertility and fine gardens. Its people denied God's blessing, so He sent the flood upon them, and in place of fertility He gave them barren land, in place of abundance hardship, and in place of richness bitterness, so that they could obtain their food only from distant places. The meaning of "ayādī" is blessings, and "ayādī Saba'" is a metaphor (isti'āra) for the states of his own self, which resemble the states of Saba' in dispersal and disturbance.)

Or it is a simile (tashbīh) of which the eloquence is disputed. In it there is a metaphor by ellipsis (majāz bi'l-ḥadhf), meaning: "the blessings of the people of Saba' which I was after you," that is, "the states I was characterised by were like the states of Saba'." It is permissible that "mā" is a verbal noun (maṣdariyya), meaning: my existence and my states after you are like the states of Saba'. Or the meaning of "ayādī Saba'" is its people who used to cultivate it, who scattered themselves by their own hands, so he likened himself to them for his lack of stability. "Saba'" is also applied to a tribe that inhabited it. It is possible that this is intended here, indeed it is more evident. It is also permissible that the intended is their father, who is Saba' ibn Yashjub ibn Ya'rub ibn Qahtan. He had wealth and sons, and his sons dispersed, some to Yemen and some to al-Sham and other places, so the "ayādī" was applied to them, because their strength was through them, like hands, and then he likened himself to them in scattering.

"ʿan" is a diminutive (murakhkham), and in calling her there is a sense of grief and entreaty. He addressed her with the plural masculine pronoun as a mark of honour, and therefore you do not find it in places of dispraise for women. The clause of address is an interjection between the predicate and the subject. It is possible that the implied meaning is: "I am like the hands of Saba' during my being after you," so it is an interjection between the clause and the adverbial phrase connected to it.

"Ḥalā yaḥlū" like "da'ā yad'ū", and other forms are rare; he likened beauty to sweetness by the common element of pleasure. It was said: "ḥalā yuḥlā" like "riḍā yariḍā" in appearance (al-manẓar), and "ḥalā yaḥlū" in taste. What is here is from the first, so there is no metaphor. "Al-manẓar" is a verbal noun meaning the act of looking. It is permissible that "al-ḥalāwa" means beauty, and "al-manẓar" with a fatḥa means the place of looking. It is also permissible that it means looking itself, that is: "no one beautiful to my eyes except you." It is also permissible that the intended "ba'dakum" is after your departure, you and your family, so the address is to her and to her tribe. But the usages of the language support what has preceded. It is reported: "falan yaḥlu," and some claimed that "lan" may apocopate (jazm) as here, and on the view of prohibition, the final of the verb is elided for necessity or lightening.

Ghassān joined al-Sham, Anmār went to Yathrib, Judhām to Tihama, and al-Azd to Oman. ﴿Patient (ṣabbār) against sins, grateful (shakūr) for blessings﴾.

Zamakhshari's commentary (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 34, verses 20–21:

It is read ṣaddaqa, with doubling and without doubling, and Iblīs in the nominative with al-ẓann in the accusative. Whoever doubles it, then the meaning is: he confirmed his assumption about them, or found it true. Whoever lightens it, then the meaning is: he spoke the truth in his assumption, or he made his assumption come true, as in: "I did it with your utmost effort" (fa'altahu juhdaka). And it is read with Iblīs in the accusative and al-ẓann in the nominative. Whoever doubles it, then the meaning is: his assumption found it true. Whoever lightens it, then the meaning is: his assumption told him the truth when he imagined their misleading, as one says: "Your assumption has spoken truly to you" (ṣadaqaka ẓannuka). And with lightening and both in the nominative, the meaning is: the assumption of Iblīs came true concerning them. If it were read with doubling and both in the nominative, it would be for emphasis in truthfulness, like his saying: "My assumptions have been truly confirmed about them."

The meaning is that when he found Adam weak in resolve, having inclined to his whispering, he said: "Indeed his offspring are weaker in resolve than he is," so he assumed they would follow him, and said: "I will surely mislead them, I will surely lead them astray." It is also said that he formed this assumption when God Most High informed the angels that He would place in the earth one who would cause corruption in it.

The pronoun in "upon them" (ʿalayhim) and "they followed him" (fa-ttabaʿūhu) refers either to the people of Sheba or to the children of Adam. He diminished the believers by His saying "except a group" (illā farīqan), because they are few in comparison with the disbelievers, just as He said: "Surely I will seize his offspring, except a few" (la-aḥtanikanna dhurriyyatahu illā qalīlan), and "You will not find most of them grateful" (wa-lā tajidu aktharahum shākirīn).

His authority over them, through domination and control by whispering and enticement, was for no purpose other than a sound objective and a clear wisdom: that the believer in the Hereafter be distinguished from the one who doubts it. He gave the reason for the authority as knowledge, and what is meant is what knowledge has been related to. It is read "that He may know" (liyaʿlama) in the passive voice. Ḥafīẓ (guardian) means one who watches over it; fa'īl and mufāʿil are mutually interchangeable.

Say to your polytheist people: "Call upon those whom you have worshipped besides Allah, the idols and the angels, and whom you have named by His name, just as you call upon Allah. Resort to them in whatever troubles you, just as you resort to Him, and expect their response to your supplication and their mercy just as you expect Him to respond to you and show you mercy." Then He answered them with His words: ﴿They do not possess an atom's weight, in the heavens or on the earth, of good or evil, or benefit or harm﴾, and they have no share in these two kinds, neither in creation nor in dominion, ﴿and He has no helper among them﴾. Like His saying: ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor [did I take] helpers from among them﴾ [Qur'an 18:51]: it means that they have this attribute of incapacity and remoteness from the states of lordship. So how is it valid that they be called upon as He is called upon, or hoped in as He is hoped in?

If you say: where are the two objects of ﴿zaʿama﴾ (to claim/suppose)?

I say: one of them is the omitted pronoun referring back from the relative pronoun. As for the second, it must be either ﴿min dūni llāh﴾ (besides Allah), or ﴿lā yamlikūna﴾ (they do not possess), or omitted. The first is not valid, because your saying "they are besides Allah" does not form a complete sentence; nor is the second, because they did not claim that, so how would they speak with what is a proof against them, and what, if they had said it, would be a truth and an affirmation of monotheism? So it remains that it is omitted, its estimate being: "you claimed them to be gods besides Allah." The pronoun returning to the relative was omitted, as it is omitted in His saying ﴿Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?﴾ [Qur'an 25:41], for lightness, because of the length of the relative clause with its complement; and ﴿āliha﴾ (gods) was omitted because it is a modified noun whose modifier is ﴿min dūni llāh﴾ (besides Allah), and a modified noun may be omitted with its modifier put in its place when it is understood. Thus the two objects of ﴿zaʿama﴾ are both omitted, for two different reasons.

You say: "The intercession is for Zayd," meaning that he is the one interceding, just as you say "The generosity is for Zayd." Or it means that he is the one for whom intercession is made, just as you say "The standing (qiyam) is for Zayd." So His saying, "And intercession does not benefit with Him except for whom He permits" (wa la tanfa'u al-shafa'atu 'indahu illa li-man adhina lahu), may be understood according to either of these two aspects. That is: intercession does not benefit except when it is made by the intercessors who have been permitted, and directed toward the one for whom it is permitted.

Or: intercession does not benefit except when it is directed to the one for whom He has permitted, i.e., to his intercessor; or it is the second lam in your saying "He permitted Zayd for 'Amr," i.e., for his sake. It is as if it were said: "except for the one for whom the permission has been granted to the intercessor." This is a subtle aspect, and it is the preferred one. This is also a refutation of their saying, "These are our intercessors with God."

If you ask: with what is His saying "until, when the fear is removed from their hearts" (hatta idha fuzzi'a 'an qulubihim) connected, and why is "until" (hatta) placed as a limit? I say: it is connected with what is understood from this statement, namely that there is a waiting for permission, an expectation, a delay, and a state of fear among those who hope for intercession and the intercessors: whether they will be permitted or not. And that permission is not granted except after a long period of time and a prolonged waiting. A state like this is indicated by the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: "Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, the Most Merciful; they do not possess speech with Him. The day the Spirit and the angels stand in rows, they will not speak except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted, and who says what is right" (Q. 78:37–38). It is as if it were said: they wait and stop, all of them fearful and terrified, until, when the fear is removed from their hearts, i.e., when the fear is lifted from the hearts of the intercessors and those for whom intercession is made, by a word spoken by the Lord of Majesty in granting permission, they rejoice at that, and some of them ask others: "What has your Lord said?" They say: "He has said the truth," i.e., the true word, which is the permission to intercede for whomever He is pleased with.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "When He permits whoever is permitted to intercede, the intercession relieves his fear" [[I have not found it]]. It is also read "udhina lahu" (with the verb passive, "permission was granted to him," i.e., Allah permitted him), and "adhina lahu" in the passive form. Al-Hasan read "fuzza'" with a light (non-doubled) z, meaning "fazi'a" (was afraid/alarmed). It is also read "fuzzi'a" in the active form, where the subject is Allah alone, and "furri'a," meaning: He removed the dread from them and annihilated it, from the expression "faragha al-zad" when no provision remained of it. Then the mention of the dread was omitted and the verb was attributed to the prepositional phrase, as you say "dufi'a ila Zayd" when it is known what was pushed. It may also be lightened, and its origin is "faragha al-wajl 'anha" (the dread departed from them), meaning it ceased and was extinguished; then the subject was deleted and the verb attributed to the prepositional phrase. It is also read "ifrannaqa 'an qulubihim," meaning: it was uncovered from them. "He is the Most High, the Great" (wa huwa al-'Aliyyu al-Kabir): possessor of exaltedness and greatness; no king or prophet may speak on that day except by His permission, and none may intercede except for whom He is pleased with.

He was commanded to put the question to them with His words, "Who provides for you?" and then he was commanded to take on the answer and the affirmation on their behalf with His words: "God provides for you." This is to indicate that they affirm it in their hearts, though they may refuse to speak it, because the stubbornness and love of polytheism that has taken hold of their breasts has bridled their mouths from uttering the truth, even though they know it to be correct. And because if they were to blurt out that God is their provider, it would follow that they be told: "Then why do you not worship the One who provides for you, and why do you prefer over Him one who has no power to provide?" Do you not see His words, "Say: Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth, or who owns hearing and sight?" up to His words, "They will say: God." Then He said, "So what is there after the truth but error?" It is as though they would affirm it with their tongues at one time, and at another time they would stammer out of obstinacy, harm, and fear of being bound by the proof. Similar to this is His words, mighty and majestic: "Say: Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth? Say: God. Say: Have you then taken besides Him protectors who have no power to benefit or harm themselves?" And He commanded him to say to them, after the binding and the bridling, which, if it added nothing beyond their affirmation with their tongues, would not fall short of it: "And indeed we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error." Its meaning: Indeed one of the two groups, those who single out the Provider from the heavens and the earth for worship, and those who associate with Him the inanimate thing that is not described as having power, is surely upon one of the two states, guidance or error. This is of the fair speech which everyone who hears it, whether a supporter or an opponent, says to the one addressed by it: "Your companion has been fair to you." And in its gradation, after the forceful affirmation that has preceded it, there is an evident indication of who is among the two groups upon guidance and who is in clear error. But allusion and indirection are more effective (anḍal) for the disputant toward the goal, more forceful in bringing about victory, with less clamor from the opponent and the breaking of his thorn without effort. Similar to this is the statement of a man to his companion: "God knows which of us is truthful, and that one of us is surely a liar."

Mahmud said: "When he had bound them with the proof in His words, 'Say: Call upon those whom you claim besides God; they do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth, nor do they have any share in them, nor does He have any helper among them,' and so on to the verse mentioned, this binding, if it added nothing beyond their affirmation with their tongues, would not fall short of it, He commanded him to say, 'And indeed we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error.' Its meaning: that one of the two groups, the monotheists who single out the Provider from the heavens and the earth for worship, and those who associate with Him the inanimate thing that has no power over an atom, is surely upon one of the two states, guidance or error. This is of the fair speech which everyone who hears it, whether a supporter or an opponent, says to the one addressed by it: 'Your companion has been fair to you.' Allusion is more effective for the disputant toward the goal, more forceful in bringing about victory, with less clamor from the opponent and the breaking of his thorn without effort. Similar to this is the statement of a man to his companion: 'God knows which of us is truthful, and that one of us is surely a liar.' And from it is the verse of Hassan: 'Do you satirize him while you are not his equal? So may the evil of you both be a ransom for the better of you both.'"

Ahmad said: "This is a refined explanation and an agreeable elegance. I repeated it to my hearing and it gained brilliance through repetition, and my mind welcomed it as though I were slow of understanding when it benefits. It should not be denied after this, by the method that the later scholars and jurists frequently practice in their disputations and discussions, namely their saying, 'One of the two matters is necessarily binding in an indefinite manner.' This path from this valley is not far, so reflect upon it. And God is the Granter of success."

And from it is the verse of Hassan: "Do you satirize him while you are not his equal? So may the evil of you both be a ransom for the better of you both."

In the reading of Ubayy: "And indeed we or you are either upon guidance or in clear error."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 34, verse 27:

If you say: What is the meaning of His saying "Show me" (arūnī), when He knows them and recognizes them? I say: He intended by that to make them see the great error in associating partners with Allah, and to set up a comparison before their eyes between Him and their idols, so as to let them know the impossibility of likening Him to anything and of associating anything with Him. "Nay" (kallā) is a rebuke to them for their doctrine, after He had undermined it by refuting the comparison, just as Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said, ﴿Uff to you and to what you worship besides Allah﴾, after he had argued against them. He has also drawn attention to the gross magnitude of their error, though they do not measure Allah with His true measure, by His saying ﴿He is Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾, as if He had said: Where are those whom you have joined with Him as partners, possessing these attributes? And this refers to Allah alone. Or the pronoun is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Say: He is Allah, One﴾.

﴿Except as a comprehensive messenger to mankind﴾ (illa kaffatan lil-nas). This means a general message that encompasses them, for once it includes them, it has restrained (kaffat) them from anyone among them going outside of it.

Al-Zajjaj (d. 311 AH) said: The meaning is, "We have sent you gathering the people together in warning and conveying the message." So he made كَافَّةً (kaffatan) a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl, an accusative expressing the state of the subject or object) of the pronoun in الكاف (al-kāf, the "kāf" of "arsalnāka," "We sent you"). On this view, the ta' in كَافَّةً is for intensification (ta' al-mubālagha), like the ta' in رَاوِيَة (rāwiya, a great transmitter) and عَلَّامَة (allāma, a great scholar).

As for one who makes it a ḥāl of the preceded genitive-marked noun (al-majrūr), he has erred. The reason is that placing the ḥāl of a genitive-marked noun before it is, in terms of reference (al-iḥāla), like placing a genitive-marked noun before its preposition. How often you see someone commit this error and yet not fall into it unless he adds to it making the lām (in لِلنَّاسِ, "to mankind") mean إِلَى (ilā, "to"). For the first error does not hold together for him except with the second error. So he must commit both errors.

Recited: "mī'ād yawmin" (mī'ād yawmin), "mī'ādu yawmin," and "mī'āda yawman." Al-mī'ād is the vessel of a promise, whether of place or of time, and here it is time. The evidence for this is the reading of whoever recited "mī'ād yawmin," where "al-yawm" is put in apposition to it (badal). If you ask: what is the interpretation of the one who made it genitive by annexation to "yawm," or put "yawman" in the accusative? I say: as for the annexation, it is an annexation of specification (idafat tabyīn), as you say "suḥq thawb" (a garment of ruin/rags) and "baʿīr sāniyah" (a water-camel). As for putting "al-yawm" in the accusative, it is for magnification (al-taʿẓīm), by supposing a verb whose estimate is: "For you there is a appointment, I mean a day," or "I intend a day whose description is such and such." The nominative may also be permissible on this basis, namely the magnification. If you ask: how does this fit as an answer to their question? I say: they asked about it only while denying it, out of obstinacy and not seeking guidance, so the answer came in the manner of a threat, corresponding to the coming of the question in the manner of denial and obstinacy, and that they are kept in wait for a day that will surprise them, so they can neither delay from it nor advance before it.

Al-ladhi bayna yadayhi (the one before it): what was revealed before the Qur'an of the books of Allah. It is related that the disbelievers of Makkah asked the People of the Book, and they informed them that they find the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in their books. This angered them, and they joined to the Qur'an all that preceded it of the books of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in disbelief. So they disbelieved in all of them. It was also said: "al-ladhi bayna yadayhi" refers to the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is: they denied that the Qur'an is from Allah, the Exalted, and that what it indicates regarding the return for recompense is a reality. Then He informed about the outcome of their affair and their final state in the Hereafter, and said to His Messenger (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him, or to the addressee:

﴿And if you could see when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord, sending back the statement among themselves...﴾ [You would see something amazing]. [Note: his words "لرأيت العجيب" (you would have seen the amazing) is perhaps "العجب" (the wonder), as in the phrasing of al-Nasafi. (Editor's note)]

So the answer is omitted. Al-mustad'afun (the oppressed/weak): they are the followers, and al-mustakbirun (the arrogant): they are the leaders and the foremost.

The first word, "nahnu" (we), is the interrogative particle of denial, because the purpose is to deny that they were the ones who barred them from faith, and to establish that they themselves turned away from it, and that they came to that by their own choice. It is as if they said: ﴿Did we compel you and come between you and your being able and free to choose, after it had come to you?﴾ after you had resolved to enter faith and your intentions were sound in choosing it? Rather, you prevented yourselves from its share, you preferred misguidance to guidance, and you obeyed the command of desire rather than the command of restraint. So you were criminals and disbelievers by your own choice, not by our word and our enticement.

If you say: "idh" (when) and "idha" (whenever) are adverbs (ẓarf) that necessarily take the sense of place, so why was "idh" made an object of a preposition? I say: the usage with time has been extended in a way it has not been with other things, so time has been attached to it, just as it is attached to clauses in your saying: "I came to you after idh the man came," and "ḥīnadhin" (then), "yawmadhin" (on that day), "kāna dhālika awān al-Ḥajjāj amīr" (that was the time when al-Ḥajjāj was governor), and "ḥīn kharaja Zayd" (when Zayd went out).

When the arrogant denied, by their saying ﴿Did we bar you from guidance?﴾, that they were the cause of the disbelief of the weak, and affirmed, by their saying ﴿Rather, you were criminals﴾, that this was by their own earning and choice, the weak turned back against them, saying ﴿Rather, it was the scheming of the night and the day﴾, and so they nullified their retraction (iḍrāb) with their own retraction. It is as if they said: "Criminality did not come from our side; rather, it came from your constant scheming against us night and day, and your compelling us to associate partners with God and take rivals."

The meaning of "the scheming of the night and the day" is: your scheming during the night and the day. The adverb has been extended by treating it as a direct object (mafʿūl bihi) and attributing the scheming to it. Or their night and day are made the schemers, by way of metaphorical attribution (isnād majāzī).

It has been read as "bal makru al-layli wa al-nahar" with tanwīn (nunation) and the two adverbs in the accusative. It has also been read as "bal makarru al-layli wa al-nahar" with the first word in the nominative and the second in the accusative. The meaning is: "You constantly persist in leading astray, a scheming that never ceases." If you ask: what is the grammatical basis of the nominative and accusative? I say: the word is either a subject (mubtada') or a predicate (khabar), meaning: "Rather, the cause of that is your scheming, or your scheming-persisting, or your scheming is the cause of that." The accusative reading means: "Rather, you persist in leading astray, a scheming of night and day."

If you ask: why was it said ﴿The arrogant said﴾ without a conjunction, while it was said ﴿And the weak said﴾? I say: because the weak had already spoken earlier, the answer was given without a conjunction, in the manner of resumption (istiʾnāf), and then another statement by the weak was added, so it is conjoined to their first statement.

If you ask: who is the referent of the pronoun in ﴿And they concealed﴾? I say: it is the group that includes both kinds, the arrogant and the weak, and they are the wrongdoers in His saying ﴿When the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord﴾. The arrogant will regret their misguidance and their misleading of others, and the weak will regret their misguidance and their following of those who misled them. ﴿On the necks of those who disbelieved﴾ means on their necks. He used the explicit term to disparage them and to indicate what made them deserve the shackles. It is reported from Qatādah: they concealed the speech about that among themselves. It has also been said: they concealed the regret and then displayed it, and this is one of the words with opposite meanings (ḍiddād).

I say: the usage with time has been extended in a way it has not been with other things, so time has been attached to it, just as it is attached to clauses in your saying: "I came to you after idh the man came," and "ḥīnadhin" (then), "yawmadhin" (on that day), "kāna dhālika awān al-Ḥajjāj amīr" (that was the time when al-Ḥajjāj was governor), and "ḥīn kharaja Zayd" (when Zayd went out).

When the arrogant denied, by their saying ﴿Did we bar you from guidance?﴾, that they were the cause of the disbelief of the weak, and affirmed, by their saying ﴿Rather, you were criminals﴾, that this was by their own earning and choice, the weak turned back against them, saying ﴿Rather, it was the scheming of the night and the day﴾, and so they nullified their retraction (iḍrāb) with their own retraction. The meaning of "the scheming of the night and the day" is: your scheming during the night and the day. The adverb has been extended by treating it as a direct object (mafʿūl bihi) and attributing the scheming to it. Or their night and day are made the schemers, by way of metaphorical attribution (isnād majāzī).

It has been read as "bal makru al-layli wa al-nahar" with tanwīn (nunation) and the two adverbs in the accusative. It has also been read as "bal makarru al-layli wa al-nahar" with the first word in the nominative and the second in the accusative. The meaning is: "You constantly persist in leading astray, a scheming that never ceases." If you ask: what is the grammatical basis of the nominative and accusative? I say: the word is either a subject (mubtada') or a predicate (khabar), meaning: "Rather, the cause of that is your scheming, or your scheming-persisting, or your scheming is the cause of that." I say: because the weak had already spoken earlier, the answer was given without a conjunction, in the manner of resumption (istiʾnāf), and then another statement by the weak was added, so it is conjoined to their first statement.

I say: it is the group that includes both kinds, the arrogant and the weak, and they are the wrongdoers in His saying ﴿When the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord﴾. It has also been said: they concealed the regret and then displayed it, and this is one of the words with opposite meanings (ḍiddād).

God Most High has refuted their assumption by showing that provision is a bounty from God, which He apportions as He wills according to what He sees as beneficial. God Most High says: ﴿And as for him whose provision is restricted (qudira 'alayhi rizquhu)...﴾ It is also read as yuqaddir, with shaddah and without shaddah.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 34, verse 37–38:

He meant: "Neither your wealth nor your children are that which brings you near." This is because the broken plural (jam' mukassar), whether its referents are rational or non-rational, is treated the same in terms of feminine agreement. It is also permissible that "al-latī" (that which) refers to piety (al-taqwā), which alone brings one near to God in closeness (zulfā); that is: your wealth is not that thing placed for bringing near.

Al-Hasan read: "bi-l-lātī tuqarribukum" (with the feminine plural relative), because they are groups (jamā'āt). It was also read: "bi-l-ladhī yuqarribukum," meaning: "with the thing which brings you near."

Al-zulfā and al-zulfa are like al-kubrā and al-kurba. Its position is in the accusative (naṣb), meaning: "it brings you near as a bringing near" (qurba), like His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And He produced you from the earth as a growth (nabātan)﴾. The exception ﴿except for one who believes﴾ is a substitution from the "kum" in "tuqarribukum." The meaning is: wealth does not bring anyone near except the believer, the righteous one, who spends it in the way of God; and children do not bring anyone near except one whose children taught them good, gave them understanding in religion, and guided them toward righteousness and obedience.

"Jazā' al-ḍi'f" (the recompense of double) is an idafa of the verbal noun (maṣdar) to its object. Its original form was: ﴿Those, for them is the recompense of being repaid double﴾, then "jazā' al-ḍi'f," then "jazā' al-ḍi'f." The meaning of "jazā' al-ḍi'f" is: their good deeds are multiplied for them, one becoming ten.

It was also read: "jazā' al-ḍi'f," on the reading: "for them double is the recompense," and "jazā' al-ḍi'f" on the reading: "they are repaid double"; both are in the nominative, with "al-ḍi'f" in apposition (badal) to "jazā'."

It was read "fī al-ghurufāt" with the rā' vowelled with ḍamma, with fatḥa, and with sukūn, and "fī al-ghurfa" (singular).

Therefore He replaces it: "fa-huwa yukhlifuhu" (He compensates for it), with no one else able to compensate. This happens either swiftly, through wealth, or through contentment, which is a treasure that never runs out. Or it happens later, through reward, of which every other replacement is less.

It is reported from Mujahid: "Whoever has from this wealth what sustains him, let him be moderate, for provision is apportioned. Perhaps what has been apportioned to him is little, yet he spends as one who is lavish, so he spends everything in his hand and then remains in poverty for the rest of his life. Let him not misinterpret: 'Whatever you spend, He will replace it' (34:39), for this refers to the Hereafter."

The meaning of the verse: "And whatever you spend of anything, He will replace it, and He is the best of providers" (34:39). The Lord of Honour is the best of providers and the highest of them. This is because whatever one provides, other than Him, such as a ruler who provides for his soldiers, a master who provides for his slave, or a man who provides for his dependants, is from the provision of God. He causes it to flow through the hands of these people. He is the Creator of provision and the Creator of the means by which the one provided for benefits from the provision.

It is reported from some of them: "Praise be to God who has caused me to find (awjadani) [[His saying "Praise be to God who has caused me to find" (al-Hamdu lillah alladhi awjadani). In al-Sihah: wajada matlubahu, and Allah awjadahu matlubahu, meaning He granted him his object, and awjadahu, meaning: made him rich. (ʿ)]] and made me one of those who are desired. How many a person who desires does not find, and how many a person who finds does not desire."

This speech is addressed to the angels and is a rebuke to the disbelievers. It follows the well-known proverb (al-mathal al-sa'ir):

*"It is you I mean, but listen, O neighbour"*

*"O sister of the best of the desert-dwellers and the town-dwellers... what do you think of the youth of Fazarah,*
*who has begun to desire a free woman who uses much perfume? It is you I mean, so listen, O neighbour."*

It was said by Sahl ibn Malik al-Fazari, addressing the sister of Harithah ibn Lam. He had come asking for her, but did not find her brother, so she hosted him and treated him generously. He saw her in the utmost beauty and perfection, so he recited this. She replied with her verses:

*"I say to you, O youth of Fazarah: I do not seek a husband, nor debauchery.*
*Nor separation from the people of guidance, the Hārah. So depart to your people with a farewell."*

He departed, then came back and stopped with her brother again. He was handsome in appearance, so she secretly sent to him that he should propose to her. He did so, married her, and departed with her.

*Al-badw* means the desert (al-badiyah), and *al-hadarah* means the settled town (al-hadirah). What is meant is their people. *Kayf* is an interrogative noun in the accusative, functioning as the object of *tarayn* ("you see"). The meaning is: "In what state do you see the youth of this tribe?", meaning himself. In it there is an indirect allusion to proposing to her.

*Al-mu'attarah* means one who uses a great deal of perfume. The attachment of the feminine *tā'* to the pattern *mif'āl* is irregular, if it is for distinguishing the masculine from the feminine, as here. It is possible that it is for intensification (*mubālaghah*) and not for feminine marking. *Al-di'arah* means immorality, wickedness and corruption.

*Hadhihi* is a demonstrative noun (ism ishārah). Her words *bi-istihārah* mean "with completeness and absence of deficiency", or alternatively "with bewilderment and lack of guidance". It is said *istahāra al-inā'* when the vessel became full and complete, and *istahāra al-rajul* when the man was confused in his opinion.

Similar to this is His saying, ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides God"?﴾ (5:116). God, glory be to Him, knows that the angels and Jesus are free of, and innocent of, what the question directed at them implies, since it is posed in the manner of a demand for confirmation (taqrīr). The purpose is that [the questioned] would say and [the others] would say, and [He] would ask and [they] would answer, so that the rebuke becomes more severe, the reproach more forceful, and their shame greater.

It is an argument of greater binding force (ilzām). The relating of this story serves as a kindness to whoever hears it and as a deterrent to whoever it is related about.

*Al-muwālāh* is the opposite of *al-mu'ādāh* (hostility). From it is the saying: "O God, befriend whoever befriends him, and be hostile to whoever is hostile to him." It is a *mufā'alah* form from *al-walī*, which means nearness, just as *al-mu'ādāh* comes from *al-'adwā'*, which means distance. *Al-walī* applies to both the one who befriends and the one who is befriended.

The meaning is: "You are the one we befriend, apart from them, since there is no friendship between us and them." So by affirming God's friendship and the disbelievers' enmity, they declare their innocence of being pleased with their worship of them, because whoever has this attribute, his condition is incompatible with that.

﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾ (34:41). They mean the devils, since they obeyed them in worshipping other than God.

It is said: the devils took the forms of a people from among the jinn and said, "These are the forms of the angels, so worship them." It is also said: they used to enter the hollows of the idols when they were worshipped, and so they were worshipped through the worship of them.

It is recited *naḥshuruhum* (we gather them) and *naqūlu* (we say) with the *nūn* and also with the *yā'*.
