The matter on that Day belongs to Allah alone. No one there possesses benefit or harm for anyone, because that abode is an abode of reward and punishment, and the one who rewards and punishes is Allah. Its state is therefore the opposite of the state of this world, which is the abode of legal obligation (dar taklif), where people are left to themselves, harming and benefiting one another. The meaning is that on that Day there is no one who harms or benefits except Him alone. Then he mentioned His punishing the wrongdoers with His words, "And We will say to those who did wrong," conjoined (ma'tuf) to "does not possess."

The first reference is to the Prophet (ﷺ), the second to the Qur'an, and the third to the truth (al-haqq), which encompasses the entire matter of prophethood and the religion of Islam as it is. In His saying "And those who disbelieve said" (﴿وَقالَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾), in His not saying "and they said," in His saying "concerning the truth when it came to them" (﴿لِلْحَقِّ لَمَّا جاءَهُمْ﴾), and in what the two particles (al-lamayn) indicate of reference to the speakers and to that about which they spoke, and in the word "lamma" (when) and its implication of hastening to disbelief, there is evidence that the speech issued forth from great denial and intense anger, and an eloquent expression of astonishment at their affair. It is as if He said: "Those rebellious disbelievers said this, in their audacity toward God and their obstinacy toward such a clear truth before tasting it: ﴿إِنْ هذا إِلَّا سِحْرٌ مُبِينٌ﴾ ('This is nothing but clear magic')." They first passed judgment that it is magic, then they went on to describe it as manifest, evident to every intelligent person who considers it, and yet they named it magic.

We did not give them books which they study, containing proof for the validity of polytheism, nor did We send to them a warner who warns them of punishment if they do not associate partners with God, as He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Or have We sent down to them an authority, so that it speaks of what they used to associate with Him?﴾ Or [He] described them as an unlettered people, people of ignorance (jahiliyya, the pre-Islamic age of ignorance), having no religion, and having no covenant concerning the sending down of a book or the sending of a messenger, as He said: ﴿Or have We given them a Book before this, so that they hold fast to it?﴾ Thus there is no tenable basis for their denial, nor any firm doubt to rely upon, as the People of the Book say, though they are falsifiers: "We are people of books and laws, and we rely on messengers from among the messengers of God." Then He threatened them for their denial with His saying: ﴿And those who came before them denied, and these have not reached one-tenth of what We gave them, yet they denied My messengers, so how was My rejection?﴾ [Here the text reads: "And those who came before them denied, and these have not reached a tenth of what We gave those (earlier ones) of long lifespans, strength of bodies, and abundance of wealth. When they denied their messengers, My punishment came to them through destruction and annihilation, and their reliance on what they relied upon did not avail them. So what is the matter with these people?"]

It is recited as yudarrisūnahā (يدرّسونها), from al-tadrīs (repetition of study), meaning "they repeat it," or from darrasa al-kitāb and darrasa al-kutub (to study the book and the books). It is also recited as yaddarisūnahā (يدّرسونها), with the dāl doubled, which is of the form yaftaʿilūn from al-dars (study). Al-ma'shār (المعشار) is like al-mirbā' (المرباع): al-ma'shār means one-tenth, and al-mirbā' means one-quarter.

If you say: what is the meaning of "fa-kadhdhabū rusulī" (﴿they denied My messengers﴾), since it is dispensed with by His saying "And those who came before them denied"? I say: since the meaning of His saying "And those who came before them denied" is that those before them committed denial and undertook it, the denial of the messengers is made a consequence of it. A parallel is for one to say: "So-and-so undertook disbelief, so he disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ)." It is also permissible that it be connected to His saying "nor have they reached," as when you say: "Zayd has not reached a tenth of the superiority of ʿAmr, yet he claims superiority over him." ﴿So how was My rejection?﴾ That is, [the punishment] of the earlier deniers, so let them beware of its like.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 34, verse 46:

*With one thing*, meaning one single matter. He explained it with His words ﴿that you stand up﴾, taking it as an appositive (ʿatf bayan) to it. By their standing he meant either rising from the assembly of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and dispersing from their gathering in his presence, or the standing that does not mean being upright on their feet, but rather taking a firm position in the matter and rising to it with resolve. The meaning is: "I admonish you with one thing only. If you do it, you will have attained the truth and been delivered: it is that you stand up for the sake of Allah alone, ﴿in pairs and singly﴾, and then ﴿reflect﴾ upon the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) and what he brought.

As for the pair: the two of them reflect, and each presents the outcome of his thinking to his companion, and they examine it together, sincerely and fairly, with neither the pursuit of desire inclining them nor the pulse of partisan zeal stirring in them, until sound thought and correct reasoning bring them onto the highway of truth and its path. Likewise the individual: he reflects on himself with justice and equity, without being stubborn toward himself, and he presents his thinking to his intellect and mind and to what is established in him of the customs of rational people and the courses of their affairs.

What made them disperse in pairs and singly is that gathering disturbs the thoughts, blinds the insight, prevents careful consideration, and muddles speech. Moreover, in gatherings fairness diminishes, injustice multiplies, and the dust-storm of partisanship rises, so that one hears nothing but support for one's own school. He showed them, through His words ﴿there is no madness in your companion﴾, that this great matter, under which lies the sovereignty of this world and the next together, is not undertaken by anyone like this claim except one of two men: either a madman, who does not care about his disgrace when he is asked for proof and fails to provide it, indeed who does not even know what disgrace is or what the end of consequences is; or a sane man of sound intellect, qualified for prophethood, chosen from among the people of the world, who does not claim it except after its authenticity has been established to him by his proof and evidence. Otherwise, a claim to something for which the sane person has no evidence would profit him nothing. And you know that Muhammad (ﷺ) has no madness in him. Rather, you have known him to be the most sound-minded of the Quraysh, the most steady in forbearance, the keenest in intellect, the most profound in judgment, the most truthful in speech, the most pure of soul, and the most gathered of all that men are praised for and commended by. So he was deserving that you should think well of him, and give preference to the side of truth over falsehood. And if you do that, it suffices you not to demand from him that he bring you a sign; for if he brings it, it becomes clear that he is a manifest warner.

If you ask: *"What does ﴿there is no madness in your companion﴾ relate to?"* I say: it may be a new independent sentence, a reminder from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, concerning the method of reflection on the matter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It may also mean: "then reflect, so that you may know that there is no madness in your companion." Some have allowed that *mā* be interrogative. ﴿Before a severe punishment﴾, like his (peace and blessings be upon him) saying [[Mentioned earlier in al-Anbiya.]]: "I have been sent in the breezes of the Hour" [[His saying "I have been sent in the breezes of the Hour": in al-Sihah, "nasm al-rih" is its first part, when it comes gently before it becomes strong. From it the hadith: "I have been sent in the breezes of the Hour," i.e., when its beginnings started and came on. Al-nasm also means the plural of nasmah, which is the soul. (ʿ)]].

Its reward is for you: "So whatever I have asked of you as a reward, it is yours," is the answer to the conditional clause, which is His saying, "Whatever reward I have asked of you." Its implied sense is: whatever reward I have asked of you, it is yours, like His saying, "Whatever Allah opens to mankind of mercy" (Qur'an 35:2). In this there are two meanings. The first: the denial of asking for any reward at all, as a man says to his companion, "If you give me something, then take it," while he knows that he has given him nothing; he intends by it finality, by hanging the taking upon something that did not exist. The second: that by "reward" he means what he meant in His saying, "Say, I do not ask you any reward for it, except that whoever wills may take a way to his Lord" (Qur'an 25:57), and in His saying, "Say, I do not ask of you any reward for it, except love for kinship" (Qur'an 42:23). This is because taking a path to Allah is their benefit and what is good for them, and likewise love for kinship, since kinship has encompassed it and them. "And Allah is over all things a Witness" (Qur'an 34:47), Watchful, Guardian, Overseer; He knows that I do not seek a reward for my advice and my calling you to Him except from Him, and that I do not hope from you for anything.

Al-qadhf and al-ramy mean propelling the arrow or the like by pushing and thrusting (tazjiyah [[His saying "al-qadhf wa'l-ramy tazjiyat al-sahm": in al-Sihah, "zajaytu al-shay' tazjiyatan" means I pushed the thing gently. (ʿ)]]). These two words are used figuratively for the sense of casting or throwing. From this comes His saying: ﴿And He cast terror into their hearts﴾, and ﴿Throw him into the chest﴾. The meaning of ﴿He casts down the truth﴾ is that He casts it and sends it down to His prophets. Or, the falsehood is struck with it, so that it crushes it and destroys it. ﴿The Knower of the unseen﴾: the word ʿallām is in the nominative (rafʿ), which is either because it is in the position of the subject of inna (ʿallām being the subject of inna and its noun, i.e. governed by the position of inna's noun), or it is a substitute for the pronoun concealed in yaqdhifu, or it is the predicate (khabar, the predicate of a subject) of an omitted subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject). It is also read in the accusative (naṣb), as an adjective (ṣifah) of "my Lord," or in the accusative of praise. It is also read al-ghuyūb with all three vowel markings, so that al-ghuyūb is like al-buyūt, and al-ghuyūb is like al-ṣabūr. It is the matter that has become absent and has become very hidden.

Al-Hayy (the living being): either it originates an action or it restores it; so when it perishes, it has no origination or restoration left. Thus they made their saying "it neither originates nor restores" a proverb for perishing. From this is the verse of ʿUbayd:

"ʿUbayd has been left desolate of his people... today it neither originates nor restores"

[[Of ʿUbayd ibn al-Abras. Aqfara means: became empty, or ʿUbayd perished from among his people. Origination and restoration require life as a precondition, so negating them is a metaphor for negating life through death. Al-Mundhir ibn Maʾ al-Samaʾ used to come out on one day of every year and bestow gifts on everyone he met, and on another day he would kill the first person he met. On that day ʿUbayd happened to meet him. He was told: "Praise him with a poem, perhaps he will pardon you." He said: "The throat-choking (al-jarīd) has prevented poetry (al-qarīd)," meaning the choking blocked the poetry. This became a proverb, and he recited this verse afterwards in grief. In Majānī al-Adab: al-Mundhir said to him: "Recite to me: 'Aqfara min ahlihi Malhūb' (Malhūb has been left desolate of its people)." He said: "Aqfara min ahlihi ʿUbayd" (ʿUbayd has been left desolate of his people). Malhūb is the name of a place. He asked him to recite an old verse, so he understood that he intended his death, and said: "I have no power to originate a new poem, nor to restore an old one." In the hashw of the verse the zihaf al-ṭayy entered, and among the ʿilal is the qaṭʿ, so mustafʿilun became mustaʿil with the lam vowelless, and that is in his saying "ahlihi."]]

The meaning: the truth has come and falsehood has perished, as in His saying, ﴿The truth has come and falsehood has vanished﴾ [17:81]. It is reported from Ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him: The Prophet (ﷺ) entered Makkah while there were three hundred and sixty idols around the Kaʿbah, and he began to strike them with a stick of nabaʿ wood [[The phrase "fa-jaʿala yaṭʿanuhu bi-ʿawdi nabaʿatin" is perhaps "maʿahu," as in al-Nasafi's wording. (ʿ)]] saying: ﴿The truth has come and falsehood has vanished; indeed falsehood was ever bound to vanish﴾ [17:81], ﴿The truth has come, and falsehood can neither originate nor restore﴾ [[Agreed upon (muttafaq ʿalayhi), and it was previously mentioned in al-Isra'.]]. Al-Haqq (the truth): the Qur'an. It is said: Islam. It is said: the sword. It is said that al-Batil (falsehood) is Iblis, may Allah curse him, meaning: he does not originate any creation nor restore it; the originator and the one who resurrects is Allah the Exalted. It is reported from al-Hasan: "It neither originates good for its people nor restores it," meaning: it benefits them neither in this world nor in the Hereafter. Al-Zajjaj said: "What does Iblis originate or restore?" making it an interrogative. It is also said that the Shaytan is called al-Batil because he is the companion of falsehood, or because he is perishing, as he is called al-Shaytan from shaṭa, meaning to perish.

Recited also: ḍalaltu aḍillu, with the ʿayn pronounced with fatḥa as well as kasra. And ḍalaltu aḍillu, with kasra in the first and fatḥa in the second; both are dialectal variants, like ẓalaltu aẓillu and ẓalaltu aẓallu. It is also recited: iḍall, with kasra on the hamza and fatḥa on the ʿayn.

If you say: where is the contrast between His words ﴿Then I only go astray to my own detriment﴾ and His words ﴿And if I am guided, it is by what my Lord reveals to me﴾? It would have been fitting to say: "Then I only go astray to my own detriment, and if I am guided, I am guided only for it (my own soul)," as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own soul; and whoever does evil, it is against it﴾, so: ﴿whoever is guided, it is for his own soul, and whoever goes astray, he only goes astray against it﴾. Or it could be said: "Then I only go astray by means of my own soul."

I say: the two are contrasted in meaning, because whatever is upon the soul is by it, meaning: whatever is a burden upon it and harmful to it is by it and because of it, since the soul commands evil. As for what benefits it, it comes by the guidance and enabling of its Lord. This is a general ruling for every person accountable. He (ﷺ) was only commanded to attribute it to his own self, because if the Messenger (ﷺ) is included under it, despite the greatness of his bearing and the soundness of his way, then others are more deserving of it.

﴿Indeed, He is Hearing, Near﴾: He perceives the speech of every one who goes astray and every one who is guided, and nothing of either of them is hidden from Him in His action.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 34, verse 51:

"And if you could see" — its response is omitted; meaning: you would see a tremendous matter and an awesome state. "Law" (if/if only), "idh" (when), and the verbs "fazi'u" (they were terrified), "akhadhu" (they were seized) and "huli'a baynahum" (they were prevented): all of them are in the past tense. What is meant by them is the future, because what God will do in the future is like what has already happened and occurred, owing to its certainty. The time of the terror is the time of the Resurrection and the establishment of the Hour. It has been said: it is the time of death. It has been said: it is the Day of Badr. And it is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that it was revealed concerning the sinking of the desert (khasf al-bayda'), because eighty thousand men set out to raid the Ka'bah to destroy it, and when they entered the desert, they were swallowed up by the earth. "Fa-la fawta" (so there is no escape): they cannot escape God, nor outrun Him. It has also been read as "fala fawt" (so there is no escape). "And they are seized from a near place": from the place of standing (al-mawqif) to the Fire when they are resurrected; or from the surface of the earth to its interior when they die; or from the desert of Badr to the well (al-qalib); or from beneath their feet when they are swallowed up by the earth. If you ask: upon what is His saying "wa-ukhidhu" (and they were seized) conjoined?

I say: there are two possibilities. It is conjoined to "fazi'u", meaning: they were terrified and seized, so there is no escape for them. Or it is conjoined to "la fawta" (there is no escape), in the sense of: when they were terrified they could not escape, and they were seized. It has also been read as "wa-akhadha" (and he seized), and it is conjoined to the position (mahall) of "la fawta".

Its meaning: there is no escape there, and there is a seizing there.

We believed in Him, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ), since he was mentioned in His saying ﴿There is no madness in your companion﴾. Al-tanawush and al-tanawul (reaching for something) are close in meaning, but al-tanawush is an easy reaching for something near. One says *nashahu yanushuhu* and *tanawashahu al-qawm*, and it is said: *tanawashu fi al-harb*, meaning some of them reached for others in battle. This is a figurative image of their seeking what cannot be attained, namely that their faith would benefit them at that time as the faith of the believers benefits them in this world. Their situation is depicted as that of a man who wants to take hold of something from a *ghalwa* (a distance of one shot), while another takes it easily from an arm's length away without any effort.[[Al-Sihah says: "*Ghalawtu bi al-sahm ghalwan*" means I shot the arrow as far as I could. *Al-ghalwa* is the limit, the distance of a shot. It also says: "It is said, between them is the length of a spear and the measure of a spear," meaning the measure of a spear's length. (Ayn)]]

It is read *al-tanawu'* (with a hamza), where the damma-marked waw was turned into a hamza, as in *ajuh* and *adu'ar*. From Abu 'Amr: *al-tanawu'* with a hamza means reaching from afar, from the saying *na'asha*, when one is slow and late. From this is the verse:

*Tamanna nu'ayshan an yakuna ata'anī*
*wa-mawlā 'asānī wa-istabadda bi-ra'yihi*
*kamā lam yuta' fīmā ashāra Qusayru*

*Fa-lammā ra'ā mā ghabba amrī wa-amruhu*
*wa-nā'at bi-a'jāzi al-umūri ṣudūru*

*Tamannā nu'ayshan an yakūna ata'anī*
*wa-qad ḥadathat ba'da al-umūri umūru*

*(He) wished, at last, that he had obeyed me. And a master who disobeyed me and was self-willed in his opinion, just as no one obeyed Qusayr in what he advised. When he saw the outcome of my affair and his affair, and the chests were burdened by the rear ends of matters, he wished, at last, that he had obeyed me, though after matters had happened, things had occurred.*

It is by Nahshal ibn Harrī. *Istabadda* means he was independent and self-sufficient in his affair. Qusayr was a man known for good judgment, and he is the subject of *ashāra*.

The object of *yuta'* is omitted because the context indicates it, or because the verb is treated as intransitive. The more sound reading is *lam yuta'* in the passive, with Qusayr as the deputy subject, whose pronoun is the subject of *ashāra*, or the reverse, according to the disagreement in the chapter of *tanāzu'* (syntactic contention over a shared element).

*Raghiba al-amr* means he reached its end, with the vowel of the *ghayn* in *raghiba* being a kasra, that is, its consequence. *Nā'a* (with the long vowel) is originally *na'a*, which was transposed, meaning it became distant. The matter is likened to a thing that has a chest and a rear end, through the metaphor of *al-makniyya* (where only the likened thing is mentioned and an attribute of it is implied) and the attributing of these to it is *takhyīl* (imaginative representation). It is as if the beginnings of matters passed by their ends, so when the beginnings had passed, the ends appeared after being hidden. It is also said *na'asha* with a hamza when one is late.

*Nu'ayshan* is in the accusative as an adverb of time, meaning "finally," i.e., at the end of the affair. The meaning is: he wished at the end of the matter that he had obeyed my advice, when he saw that the outcome of my affair was good and the outcome of his affair was bad, while difficult matters had happened after easy ones, which were hidden and made him wish this. So this is a clarifying state (*hāl mubayyinah*) for the intended sense of the adverb. Or: difficult matters had occurred after the easy matters in which he could have obeyed me, matters that prevented him from escaping his predicament, just as I had advised him first, but he did not listen and went on with his opinion.

﴿Finally﴾, i.e., at last. *Wa-yaqdhifūna* is coordinated with *qad kafarū* in the narration of a past state. The meaning: they used to speak of the unseen and bring it ﴿from a far place﴾, which is their saying about the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "a poet, a sorcerer, a liar." This is speaking of the unseen and the hidden matter, because they had not witnessed from him any sorcery, poetry, or lying. They brought this unseen matter from a far direction in relation to his condition, because the furthest thing from what he brought is poetry and sorcery, and the furthest thing from his habit, which was known and tested among them, is lying and falsehood.

It is also read *wa-yuqadhafūna bi-al-ghayb*, with the passive construction, meaning their devils bring it to them and teach it to them. If you wish, attach it to His saying ﴿And they will say, "We believed in it"﴾, as their likeness in seeking to obtain what they had neglected of faith in this world by saying "We believed" in the Hereafter. This is a seeking that is far-fetched, like one who throws something from a far place where there is no room to think it will reach, since he wants it to land there while it is absent and distant from him. *Al-ghayb* means the absent thing.

It may also be that the pronoun refers to the severe punishment in His saying ﴿before a severe punishment﴾. They used to say: "We will not be punished, even if the matter is as you describe, regarding the Hour, punishment and reward; we are too honorable before God to be punished," measuring the matter of the Hereafter by the matter of this world. So this was their hurling of the unseen, which is unseen and hurled from a far place, because the house of recompense cannot be measured by the house of obligation.

﴿What they desire﴾ refers to the benefit of faith on that day, deliverance by it from the Fire, and success in Paradise, or to their return to this world, as He reported about them: ﴿Send us back, that we may do righteous deeds﴾.

﴿With their likes﴾, i.e., with their similars among the disbelieving nations, and whoever holds their view. ﴿Doubtful﴾ may be from *arābahu*, when it brought him into doubt and suspicion, or from *arāba al-rajul*, when he became one who has doubt and entered into it. Both are metaphorical, except that there is a difference between them: the doubtful in the first sense is transferred from one who can truly be doubtful to the meaning of the thing, while the doubtful in the second sense is transferred from the one who has doubt to the doubt itself, as you say: "a poet's poetry" (*shi'r shā'ir*).

*wa-qad ḥadathat ba'da al-umūri umūru*

*(He) wished, at last, that he had obeyed me. And a master who disobeyed me and was self-willed in his opinion, just as no one obeyed Qusayr in what he advised. When he saw the outcome of my affair and his affair, and the chests were burdened by the rear ends of matters, he wished, at last, that he had obeyed me, though after matters had happened, things had occurred.*

It is by Nahshal ibn Harrī. *Istabadda* means he was independent and self-sufficient in his affair. Qusayr was a man known for good judgment, and he is the subject of *ashāra*.

The object of *yuta'* is omitted because the context indicates it, or because the verb is treated as intransitive. The more sound reading is *lam yuta'* in the passive, with Qusayr as the deputy subject, whose pronoun is the subject of *ashāra*, or the reverse, according to the disagreement in the chapter of *tanāzu'* (syntactic contention over a shared element).

*Raghiba al-amr* means he reached its end, with the vowel of the *ghayn* in *raghiba* being a kasra, that is, its consequence. *Nā'a* (with the long vowel) is originally *na'a*, which was transposed, meaning it became distant. The matter is likened to a thing that has a chest and a rear end, through the metaphor of *al-makniyya* (where only the likened thing is mentioned and an attribute of it is implied) and the attributing of these to it is *takhyīl* (imaginative representation). It is as if the beginnings of matters passed by their ends, so when the beginnings had passed, the ends appeared after being hidden. It is also said *na'asha* with a hamza when one is late.

*Nu'ayshan* is in the accusative as an adverb of time, meaning "finally," i.e., at the end of the affair. The meaning is: he wished at the end of the matter that he had obeyed my advice, when he saw that the outcome of my affair was good and the outcome of his affair was bad, while difficult matters had happened after easy ones, which were hidden and made him wish this. So this is a clarifying state (*hāl mubayyinah*) for the intended sense of the adverb. Or: difficult matters had occurred after the easy matters in which he could have obeyed me, matters that prevented him from escaping his predicament, just as I had advised him first, but he did not listen and went on with his opinion.

﴿Finally﴾, i.e., at last. *Wa-yaqdhifūna* is coordinated with *qad kafarū* in the narration of a past state. The meaning: they used to speak of the unseen and bring it ﴿from a far place﴾, which is their saying about the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "a poet, a sorcerer, a liar." This is speaking of the unseen and the hidden matter, because they had not witnessed from him any sorcery, poetry, or lying. They brought this unseen matter from a far direction in relation to his condition, because the furthest thing from what he brought is poetry and sorcery, and the furthest thing from his habit, which was known and tested among them, is lying and falsehood.

It is also read *wa-yuqadhafūna bi-al-ghayb*, with the passive construction, meaning their devils bring it to them and teach it to them. If you wish, attach it to His saying ﴿And they will say, "We believed in it"﴾, as their likeness in seeking to obtain what they had neglected of faith in this world by saying "We believed" in the Hereafter. This is a seeking that is far-fetched, like one who throws something from a far place where there is no room to think it will reach, since he wants it to land there while it is absent and distant from him. *Al-ghayb* means the absent thing.

It may also be that the pronoun refers to the severe punishment in His saying ﴿before a severe punishment﴾. They used to say: "We will not be punished, even if the matter is as you describe, regarding the Hour, punishment and reward; we are too honorable before God to be punished," measuring the matter of the Hereafter by the matter of this world. So this was their hurling of the unseen, which is unseen and hurled from a far place, because the house of recompense cannot be measured by the house of obligation.

﴿What they desire﴾ refers to the benefit of faith on that day, deliverance by it from the Fire, and success in Paradise, or to their return to this world, as He reported about them: ﴿Send us back, that we may do righteous deeds﴾.

﴿With their likes﴾, i.e., with their similars among the disbelieving nations, and whoever holds their view. ﴿Doubtful﴾ may be from *arābahu*, when it brought him into doubt and suspicion, or from *arāba al-rajul*, when he became one who has doubt and entered into it. Both are metaphorical, except that there is a difference between them: the doubtful in the first sense is transferred from one who can truly be doubtful to the meaning of the thing, while the doubtful in the second sense is transferred from the one who has doubt to the doubt itself, as you say: "a poet's poetry" (*shi'r shā'ir*).

From the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah Saba, there will not remain a messenger or prophet except that he will be a companion and a handshaker for him on the Day of Resurrection."[[Narrated by al-Tha'labi, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Wahidi with their chains from Ubayy ibn Ka'b.]]
